l1.text: So… what actually happens to your brain when you get a concussion?

l2.text: A concussion is a type of brain injury caused by a bump, blow, or jolt to the head—or even a hit to the body that makes the brain move rapidly inside the skull.

l3.text: Even when there's no obvious damage on a scan, that sudden movement can temporarily disrupt how brain cells communicate and how the brain uses energy.

l4.text: That can lead to symptoms like headache, dizziness, fatigue, brain fog, trouble concentrating, memory problems, or sensitivity to light and noise.

l5.text: And here's something important: you do not have to lose consciousness to have a concussion. In fact, most people with concussions do not.

l6.text: Symptoms can also show up right away—or develop hours or even days later. That's why it's important to pay attention to how you're feeling after an injury.

l7.text: If you think you've had a concussion, stop the activity and get evaluated by a qualified professional.

l8.text: A concussion is a brain injury. I'm your brain—let's learn together.
